title: Mem

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tall letter, and a loud room full of questions. Your line was lamed learns. What did you ask? Today, a letter you can drink. Day one thousand three hundred forty-one.

Before there is light, before land, before anything has a name, there is water. That's how the Torah opens. The earth is without form, darkness lies over the deep, and above it all, in the King James, "the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters." Water isn't made on any of the days that follow. It's simply there, waiting, at the very start of the story. And the Hebrew word for it is a small, round word with a soft sound you make with closed lips, a sound like humming. Mayim. Today's letter opens it and closes it.
screen: `BEFORE THE LIGHT.` → `THE FACE OF THE WATERS.` → `MAYIM.`

segments.voice: Mem. Let's take it in four sips. First, the word. Mayim is spelled mem, yud, mem. The letter stands at both ends, with a little yud between, like water held in a cup. Second, the shape. Mem changes depending on where it falls. In the middle of a word, it's open at the bottom, a mem you could pour out of. At the end of a word, it closes into a square, sealed. Mayim uses both: it starts with the open mem and ends with the closed one. Some teachers like that picture: water that flows, and water that's held. Third, a name drawn out of water. In Exodus, a baby is hidden in a basket among the reeds of the river, and Pharaoh's daughter finds him. The King James gives her words: "And she called his name Moses: and she said, Because I drew him out of the water." In Hebrew his name is Moshe, and it begins with mem. The man who will one day lead the people through the sea begins his life being lifted out of a river. Fourth, the cup in your hand. Even water gets a blessing. Before drinking it, Jews who say blessings recite a short one that praises God, by whose word all things came to be. Not the blessing for wine, not the blessing for bread. A short, general one, for a plain drink. Water is easy to stop noticing. The Torah puts it on the first page, and the blessing puts a pause before every glass.
screen: `MEM, YUD, MEM.` · `OPEN MEM, CLOSED MEM.` · `DRAWN OUT OF THE WATER.` · `A BLESSING FOR A GLASS.` · then, large: `WATER, ON THE FIRST PAGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drink a glass of water slowly. If you have one nearby, pick it up. If not, bring to mind the last glass you drank, and keep this for the next one. Settle, and breathe. Look at the water first. Notice its weight in your hand, the light in it. Then take one slow sip, and follow it: in the mouth, then down. Take another, and let it take longer. If you say blessings, this is a moment for the blessing over water. If you don't, just let the glass be the whole of your attention. The bell holds the time.
Mem. The letter at both ends of mayim, water, open in the middle of a word and closed at the end. Today's word.
Your line: mem is water. Today, before one glass of water, pause for one breath, as if it were worth a blessing. Day one thousand three hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Before drinking water, observant Jews say a short blessing, the shehakol, praising God 'by whose word all things came to be'; children learning to write Hebrew are taught the open mem and the closed final mem.

original.note: Hebrew: water. Open mem (מ) at the start, closed final mem (ם) at the end.

trapdoor: what you thought: mem is just the m sound.
what it means: the letter at both ends of mayim, water.
what a scholar hears: mem has an open form and a closed final form, and mayim uses both; Exodus 2:10 ties the name Moshe to being drawn out of water.

notes: Genesis 1:2 and Exodus 2:10 quoted from the KJV (1769); JPS 1917 differs ('hovered over the face of the waters'). Confirm KJV wording; a Keeper may prefer JPS 1917.
'Water isn't made on any of the days that follow' is a reading of Genesis 1 (the waters are divided and gathered, not created); confirm framing.
The shehakol blessing paraphrased ('by whose word all things came to be'); not quoted. 'Jews who say blessings' in the teach and 'observant Jews' in howItsDone; confirm.
Open and final mem described; 'some teachers like that picture' of flowing and held water is soft; confirm.
'The man who will one day lead the people through the sea' looks ahead to Exodus 14; confirm.

Editor: 'the plainest one, for the plainest drink' (superlative) became 'a general one'; the practice no longer repeats day 1336's 'hold your hands as if around a cup' and sip wording; the fork now follows Exodus 2:10, where the naming comes after the child has grown; replaced the stock 'ordinary Tuesday' line ('the thing we notice least').
